idiom_name: kotlinx.coroutines Dispatchers.IO (limitedParallelism) over JVM NIO selectors
implementation_notes: Kotlin inherits java.nio's Selector - whose selection operations synchronise on the selector, which already gives the leader serialisation - but never hand-writes the pool: kotlinx.coroutines supplies the concurrency layer. Dispatchers.IO is documented as a shared pool "designed for offloading blocking IO tasks to a shared pool of threads", defaulting to max(64, cores) with limitedParallelism views for a dedicated budget, so blocking work leaves the readiness loop alone. Suspending I/O (a selector loop confined to one dispatcher thread, or a Netty/Ktor stack) replaces the role protocol; the classic structure is justified mainly for a small JVM-only proxy built directly on Selector, where adding a coroutine stack is not wanted.
pitfalls: Dispatchers.IO's parallelism is a soft limit - its views share threads with it and extra threads may exist while starting or shutting down - so it is not the fixed pool the classic pattern assumes.
Foreign blocking calls belong in Dispatchers.IO, not Dispatchers.Default; blocking the CPU pool starves every coroutine scheduled on it.
A Selector's selected-key set is not thread-safe: the select loop must stay on one thread even when handlers are coroutines.
Blocking inside a coroutine without withContext(io) suspends nothing; it pins the dispatcher thread and with it every socket that thread demultiplexes.
